FN1 Support: Is It a Function?

CheckIt Practice Companion

Watch a Video to Learn

A narrated walkthrough of how to decide whether a relation is a function, covering mapping diagrams, tables, ordered pairs, equations, and graphs.

The video walkthrough is coming soon. In the meantime, the Quick Summary and the Try It tabs cover the same ideas.

Quick Summary

Every FN1 question asks the same thing: can one input ever correspond to more than one output? If yes, it is not a function.

What to check in each representation
RepresentationWhat to checkNot a function when…
Mapping diagramArrows leaving each inputan input has two arrows
TableThe x-valuesan x-value repeats with a different y
Ordered pairsThe x-coordinatestwo pairs share an x but have different y
EquationThe power on \( y \)\( y \) has an even power (\( y^2, y^4 \)). With \( y \) in just one term, an odd power always gives a function
GraphThe vertical line testa vertical line crosses the graph more than once

Your CheckIt problem will have different numbers than the examples here. The reasoning is what transfers.

Try It: Mapping, Table & Ordered Pairs

Make your best guess on each one, then check it. The data under each picture lists the same information the picture shows — use it however's easiest.

Mapping Diagram

Does this mapping define a function?

The input 8 appears twice in the list — once going to 9, once going to 17. One input can't correspond to two different outputs, so this mapping does not define a function. (Every other input appears only once, so that one repeat is the whole story.)

Table

Table of x-values and y-values, listed in two rows
x4710131619
y11215839

Does this table define a function?

Scan the x-row: 4, 7, 10, 13, 16, 19 — every value appears exactly once. No input is repeated, so this table defines a function. (It doesn't matter that some y-values might repeat — only repeats in x break the definition.)

Ordered Pairs

\( (3, 9) \), \( (3, 14) \), \( (6, 2) \), \( (10, 5) \), \( (15, 8) \), \( (18, 1) \)

Do these ordered pairs define a function?

\( (3, 9) \) and \( (3, 14) \) share the same x-value, 3, but disagree on y. That's the same conflict as a repeated input in a mapping diagram — just written as coordinates. So these ordered pairs do not define a function.

Try It: Equations

For each equation, decide whether it defines \( y \) as a function of \( x \). Look at the power on \( y \).

Equation 1

\[ 3y^5 + 2x^4 = 0 \]

Does this equation define a function of \( x \)?

Solving for \( y \) here means taking a fifth root — an odd root. Odd roots are invertible, with no sign ambiguity: each real number has exactly one real fifth root. So this equation defines a function of \(x\).

Equation 2

\[ 2y^4 + 3x^5 = 0 \]

Does this equation define a function of \( x \)?

Solving for \( y \) here means taking a fourth root — an even root. Even roots aren't invertible: the fourth root can't tell you whether the original number was positive or negative, so one value of \(x\) can correspond to two values of \(y\). So this equation does not define a function of \(x\).

Try It: Graphs

Apply the vertical line test: if any vertical line would cross the graph more than once, it's not a function.

Graph 1

Does this graph represent a function?

This is the line \(y=-2x+3\). Any vertical line you draw crosses a straight (non-vertical) line exactly once. This graph represents a function.

Graph 2

Does this graph represent a function?

This is the graph of \(x=y^2-4\) — a parabola opened sideways instead of up. A vertical line through the open side of the curve crosses it twice (once above the x-axis, once below). This graph does not represent a function.

Graph 3

Does this graph represent a function?

Check the x-coordinates: \(-4, -2, 0, 2, 4\) — all five are different, so no vertical line can pass through more than one point. This graph represents a function.
